extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent attorneys (prosecution and appeals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and presenting objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness in patent prosecution (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.) and how such evidence should be weighed against a prima facie case of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action when applicant's rebuttal insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after evaluating the evidence, the examiner is still not convinced that the claimed invention is patentable, the next Office action should include a statement to that effect and identify the reason(s) (e.g., evidence of commercial success not convincing, the commercial success not related to the technology, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific reasons why proffered secondary evidence fails to overcome the prima facie case. See Demaco Corp. v. F. Von Langsdorff Licensing Ltd. and MPEP § 716.01; see MPEP § 2144.08 II.B. for guidance on sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of unexpected results — issue defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may be expected to result in some differences in properties. The issue is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is really unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether differences are 'differences in kind' (potentially probative) rather than mere 'differences in degree'. Case guidance: In re Merck & Co.; In re Waymouth; compare In re Wagner; Ex parte Gelles (discussion that 'differences in degree' vs 'in kind' have little legal meaning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must show unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater than expected result is an evidentiary factor pertinent to the legal conclusion of nonobviousness; applicants must show results were greater than those which would have been expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent, and that the results are of a significant, practical advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater-than-additive (synergistic) effects can be probative (Merck v. Biocraft) but are not necessarily sufficient because such effects can be expected; cite Ex parte The NutraSweet Co. Applicants should show practical significance and explain expectation baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of a property shared with prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unobvious or unexpected advantageous properties, such as superiority in a property the claimed compound shares with the prior art, can rebut prima facie obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No set number of examples of superiority required. Example: In re Chupp (unexpected superior herbicidal effectiveness sufficient to overcome 103 rejection despite average performance elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an unexpected property
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a property not possessed by the prior art is evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Papesch (anti-inflammatory property not possessed by prior art reversed rejection). But presence of unexpected properties does not automatically mandate nonobviousness (see In re Payne). Consider latent properties and additional advantages (MPEP § 2145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of a property which a claimed invention would have been expected to possess based on teachings of the prior art is evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ex parte Mead Johnson (claimed compounds lacked beta-adrenergic blocking activity expected from prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence relied upon should establish that the differences in results are in fact unexpected and unobvious and of both statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusions in briefs or specification are insufficient (Ex parte Gelles; Ex parte C). See In re Nolan and In re Eli Lilly for precedent and MPEP § 716.02(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants must explain proffered data
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellants/applicants have the burden of explaining the data in any declaration they proffer as evidence of non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Ex parte Ishizaka. Declarations must not be unexplained or just conclusory; provide context, methods, and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected properties may be in the form of a direct or indirect comparison of the claimed invention with the closest prior art which is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Boesch and MPEP §§ 716.02(d)-716.02(e). Proper comparative testing (commensurate in scope) can rebut prima facie obviousness; direct comparative testing often required to show unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate patentability via end-product unexpected properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product when one of ordinary skill would reasonably ascribe to the claimed intermediate the 'contributing cause' for such unexpectedly superior activity or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must identify cause of the unexpectedly superior activity in the end product and establish a nexus between the intermediate and the end product (In re Magerlein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing unexpected and expected evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results must be weighed against evidence supporting prima facie obviousness in making the final determination of obviousness of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected properties must have significance equal to or greater than expected properties to rebut obviousness (In re May; In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly). See MPEP § 716.01(d) on weighing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness of a claimed invention, just as unexpected results are evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art teaches that a result would be expected, evidence of that expected result supports a finding of obviousness (In re Gershon; Ex parte Blanc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective evidence of non-obviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; the showing must be reviewed to see if results occur over the entire claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Clemens (tests at only high 'elevated' temps insufficient when claims cover lower temps); In re Grasselli (tests limited to sodium not commensurate with broader claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness of a genus supported by species under circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonobviousness of a broader claimed range or genus can be supported by evidence based on unexpected results from testing a narrower range or species if one of ordinary skill can determine a trend allowing reasonable extension of probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Kollman and In re Lindner for limits; limited exemplified species insufficient unless data show trend or extension is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Hill for requirement to demonstrate criticality with comparative testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration must compare with closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison of claimed invention with each cited reference to determine number and relative importance of claim limitations usually yields the closest single prior art reference (In re Burckel; In re Merchant). Deviations from reference disclosures should be explained (In re Finley; In re Armstrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention may be compared with closer prior art than examiner used
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may compare the claimed invention with prior art that is more closely related to the invention than the prior art relied upon by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such comparisons can be probative to rebut examiner's prima facie case (In re Holladay; Ex parte Humber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons when there are two equally close prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing unexpected results over one of two equally close prior art references will not rebut prima facie obviousness unless the teachings of the references are sufficiently similar that testing one provides the same information as to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Johnson: where applicant tested less than all cited compounds, testing must be sufficient to permit conclusions about relative effectiveness across the references (quoting In re Payne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare only with closest subject matter that exists in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant is not required to compare the claimed invention with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art (i.e., hypothetical combinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that compares with the most relevant prior art is acceptable; courts have rejected requirement to compare with inventions that would only result from combining references (In re Geiger; In re Chapman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages disclosed or inherent in specification considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of the record must be considered; evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded solely because they were not in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of advantages not disclosed may be relevant during prosecution give-and-take (In re Chu). Specification need not disclose proportions/values as critical for applicants to present evidence showing criticality (In re Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration or affidavit form requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations/affidavits under 37 CFR 1.132 are required to obtain assurances that statements are correct; publications may be evidence but do not substitute for sworn testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting a publication to substitute for expert testimony would circumvent statutory guarantees (Ex parte Gray). Publications may be considered if probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success requires nexus to claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence of commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO relies on applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success and nexus (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). Nexus means a factually and legally sufficient connection (Demaco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success abroad is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success abroad, as well as in the United States, is relevant in resolving the issue of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Lindemann Maschinenfabrik GMBH v. American Hoist & Derrick Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims; commercial success must be due to claimed features and not to unclaimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of sales of broadly claimed categories (e.g., 'containers') that do not match claimed scope (e.g., 'cups') will be insufficient (In re Tiffin). Dependent-claim features responsible for success do not support broader independent claims (Joy Technologies v. Manbeck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit language alone insufficient to show nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration attributing commercial success to a product 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' does not establish nexus because it lacks evidence that sold product corresponds to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Standish: provide concrete evidence linking claimed features to commercial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be derived from claimed invention, not marketing or extraneous factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine that alleged commercial success is directly derived from the invention in a marketplace where consumers choose on objective principles, and not the result of heavy promotion, advertising, brand loyalty, favorable licensing conditions, or other business events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusive statements attributing sales to the invention are little weight (In re Mageli; In re Noznick). Inventor's opinion insufficient to demonstrate nexus (In re Huang). Consider alternative explanations such as advertising, market shifts, licensing economics (Pentec; EWP Corp.; Hybritech example where advertising still allowed nexus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success of embodiments may not be attributable to modifications by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show success ties to claimed features or inherent properties (In re Vamco Machine & Tool).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing nexus especially difficult in design patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design itself rather than to brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cases require clear attribution to the design (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined to show commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures do not show commercial success absent evidence as to market share, time period of sales, or what sales would normally be expected in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide market share data, defined time periods, and baselines for expected sales (Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need and failure of others — criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must satisfy a long-felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not solved by others; objective evidence that an art-recognized problem existed for a long period without solution is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Need must have been recognized by those of ordinary skill; prior solutions destroy the 'long-felt need' argument (Newell Cos. v. Kenney Mfg.). See Orthopedic Equipment example where no evidence of unsuccessful attempts existed. Also consider other reasons failure occurred (lack of interest, lack of appreciation) (Scully Signal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need is measured from date problem identified and efforts made
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-felt need is analyzed as of the date the problem is identified and articulated, and there is evidence of efforts to solve it, not as of the date of the most pertinent prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Texas Instruments v. Int’l Trade Comm’n for timing of analysis.
